pride_data.title: Characterizing protein conformers by cross-linking mass spectrometry and pattern recognition
pride_data.projectDescription: Motivation: Chemical cross-linking coupled to mass spectrometry (XLMS) emerged as a powerful technique for studying protein structures and large-scale protein-protein interactions. Nonetheless, XLMS lacks software tailored toward dealing with multiple conformers; this scenario can lead to high-quality identifications that are mutually exclusive. This limitation hampers the applicability of XLMS in structural experiments of dynamic protein systems, where less abundant conformers of the target protein are expected in sample. Results: We present QUIN-XL, a software that uses unsupervised clustering to group cross-link identifications by their quantitative profile across multiple samples. QUIN-XL highlights regions of the protein or system presenting changes in its conformation when comparing different biological conditions. We demonstrate the usefulness of our software by revisiting the HSP90 protein, comparing three of its different conformers. QUIN-XL’s clusters correlate directly to known protein 3D structures of the conformers and therefore validates our software.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: The HSP90 protein used for the experiments was the human one, analyzed in a purified solution with the nucleotides being added separately afterwards for the formation of complexes. This way, each of the samples should be enriched for a different conformer. The nucleotides were ADP and ATP-γ-S (referenced in the text as ATP), which is a more stable analog of ATP and does not hydrolyze immediately. The cross-linker used was DSS dissolved in DMF (final concentration of 27mmol/L) in a molar excess of 100 times relative to the protein concentration. The cross-link reactions occurred for 2 hours at 27°C. Reducing of the disulfide bonds was done by adding 20μL of a 10mmol/L solution of DTT (prepared in a 100mmol/L buffer solution of ammonium bicarbonate) and incubating it for 30 minutes at 70°C. Alkylation of thiol groups was done by adding 20μL of a 50mmol/L solution of iodoacetamide (prepared in a 100mmol/L ammonium bicarbonate buffer solution) and incubating it for 30 minutes in the dark at room temperature. The cross-linked proteins were digested using trypsin in a proportion of 1:50 (w/w) enzyme:substrate for 18 hours at 37°C. Mass spectrometry data for HSP90 was generated in the following conditions: a) ATP-bound, b) ADP-bound, and c) nucleotide-free (Apo). Digested samples sample were analyzed in two technical replicates using an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid (ThermoFisher Scientific) mass spectrometer coupled with an Easy nLC 1200 chromatography system. Each sample was analyzed in 40 minutes chromatography, using linear gradients set as follows: 5 to 30% B (v/v)  (with solvent B: acetonitrile + 0.1% formic acid (v/v)) from 0 to 20 minutes, 30 to 90%  B from 20 to 35 minutes, then 90% B from 35 to 40 minutes. Instrument method was set up in DDA mode, HCD fragmentation with stepped collision energy from 30 to 34. Survey scans were acquired at resolution 60,000. Precursor selection was performed by cycle time with maximum injection time of 250 ms, and 8 seconds dynamic exclusion window. Precursor ions with charge 3+ to 8+ were selected for fragmentation. MS2 spectra were acquired with resolution 30,000.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: The search for the cross-links in each condition was made using the software Spectrum Identification Machine for Cross-linked Peptides (SIM-XL) (Lima et al., 2018), with the following parameters: • Cross-linker: DSS • Precursor ppm (MS1): 10 • Fragment ppm (MS2): 20 • Modifications: Carbamidomethylation of cysteine • Enzyme: Trypsin • Enzyme specificity: Fully specific • Number of isotopic possibilities: 4 • Minimum number of amino acids per chain: 4 • Intra-link maximum charge: 4 • Maximum number of missed cleavages: 3
